items.followUp: How does increasing the surface area of a liquid affect its rate of evaporation?

rubric.why: Recognises that heating gives liquid particles more kinetic energy, so more can escape from the surface.
rubric.description: Explains how higher temperature affects liquid particles.
rubric.how: Award for stating that particles gain kinetic energy or move faster.

rubric.why: States the resulting increase in evaporation.
rubric.description: States the effect on the rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award for saying evaporation becomes faster or its rate increases.

modelAnswer: As temperature increases, liquid particles gain kinetic energy and move faster.
More particles can escape from the surface, so the rate of evaporation increases.

items.followUp: Define percentage mass/volume and write its formula.

rubric.why: Identifies the mass of solute compared with a fixed volume of the solution.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that it is the mass of solute, in grams, present in 100 mL (or cm³) of solution.

rubric.why: Gives the calculation used to express the concentration as % m/v.
rubric.how: Award for the equivalent of (mass of solute in g ÷ volume of solution in mL) × 100.

modelAnswer: Percentage mass/volume is the number of grams of solute present in 100 mL of solution.
% m/v = (mass of solute in g ÷ volume of solution in mL) × 100.

items.followUp: State two differences between a true solution and a colloid.

rubric.why: The Tyndall effect is a characteristic property of colloids.
rubric.how: Award for naming the Tyndall effect or saying colloidal particles scatter a beam of light.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles remain dispersed rather than settling on standing.
rubric.description: States that colloidal particles do not settle on standing.
rubric.how: Award for saying the particles remain suspended or do not settle.

modelAnswer: Colloidal particles scatter a beam of light; this is called the Tyndall effect.
Colloidal particles do not settle down on standing and remain dispersed.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a saturated solution and an unsaturated solution.

rubric.why: A dilute solution has relatively little solute for a given amount of solution or solvent.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it contains a relatively small amount of solute in a fixed amount of solution or solvent.

rubric.why: A concentrated solution has relatively much solute for a given amount of solution or solvent.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it contains a relatively large amount of solute in a fixed amount of solution or solvent.

modelAnswer: A dilute solution contains a relatively small amount of solute in a given amount of solution (or solvent).
A concentrated solution contains a relatively large amount of solute in the same amount of solution (or solvent).

items.followUp: What is an alloy? Give one example other than brass.

rubric.why: An alloy is a mixture, generally homogeneous, of two or more elements with at least one metal.
rubric.how: Award for identifying an alloy as a mixture of metals, or a homogeneous mixture of elements with at least one metal.

rubric.why: Brass is a familiar alloy of copper and zinc.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of an alloy.
rubric.how: Award for brass, steel, bronze, or another correct alloy; accept its constituent elements where identified correctly.

modelAnswer: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal with another element.
Brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, is an example.

items.followUp: What happens to an electrolyte when it dissolves in water?

rubric.why: Hydrochloric acid is a strong electrolyte.
rubric.description: Gives one example of a strong electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award for one correct example, such as HCl.

rubric.why: Sodium hydroxide and sodium chloride are strong electrolytes.
rubric.description: Gives a second example of a strong electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award for a second distinct correct example, such as NaOH or NaCl.

modelAnswer: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is a strong electrolyte.
Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is another example of a strong electrolyte.

rubric.why: Electropositivity describes the tendency to give up electrons.
rubric.description: Identifies the tendency involved in electropositivity.
rubric.how: Award for stating that an atom tends to lose or donate electrons.

rubric.why: Loss of electrons produces positively charged ions.
rubric.description: States the result of losing electrons.
rubric.how: Award for stating that this forms positive ions or cations.

modelAnswer: Electropositivity is the tendency of an atom to lose or donate electrons.
By losing electrons, the atom forms a positively charged ion (cation).

items.followUp: State three conclusions drawn from Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment.

rubric.why: Most alpha particles passed through the foil without deflection.
rubric.description: Reports the main observation for most alpha particles.
rubric.how: Award for stating that most alpha particles passed straight through the foil.

rubric.why: A small fraction of alpha particles underwent slight deflection.
rubric.description: Reports the observation of slight deflections.
rubric.how: Award for stating that some particles were deflected through small angles.

rubric.why: Only a very small number were strongly deflected.
rubric.description: Reports the observation of large-angle deflections.
rubric.how: Award for stating that very few particles were deflected through large angles.

rubric.why: An extremely small number were reflected back; textbooks commonly state about one in 8000.
rubric.how: Award for stating that about one in 8000 rebounded or that a particle was deflected back through about 180°.

rubric.why: The scattering results led to the conclusion that the atom is mostly empty space with its positive charge concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus.
rubric.description: Gives a conclusion from the observations.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the mostly empty atom or the tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus.

modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without deflection, showing that most of the atom is empty space.
Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
A very few alpha particles were deflected through large angles.
About one alpha particle in 8000 rebounded, turning back through nearly 180°.
The deflections showed that nearly all the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus.
